subject: chemistry

moments.title: Guldberg and Waage formalise
moments.body: Two Norwegian brothers-in-law publish the law of mass action: the rate of a reaction is proportional to the concentrations of reactants. The paper is in Norwegian; it is ignored for 13 years.
moments.takeaway: The first quantitative law of chemical equilibrium, in an obscure Norwegian journal.

moments.title: Le Chatelier's principle
moments.body: A mining engineer formulates a qualitative principle: 'If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to oppose the disturbance.' The principle is widely used in chemistry teaching ever since.
moments.takeaway: A simple qualitative principle to predict reaction shifts.

moments.title: Haber-Bosch ammonia
moments.body: Haber demonstrates ammonia synthesis from N2 and H2 at high pressure and temperature, using an osmium catalyst. Bosch scales it for industry at BASF. Le Chatelier's principle is applied at industrial scale — Haber wins the 1918 Nobel, Bosch in 1931.
moments.takeaway: Le Chatelier's principle feeds half the world.

moments.title: Nitrogen for the planet
moments.body: The Haber-Bosch process now fixes ~200 million tonnes of N per year — about half of the nitrogen in human bodies came from a Haber-Bosch reactor. It uses 1-2% of all global energy.
moments.takeaway: Le Chatelier's principle keeps the world fed.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Equilibrium calculations are central to industrial chemistry, biochemistry and climate science. Catalysis aims for green Haber-Bosch with renewable hydrogen.
now.open_questions: Can low-pressure, low-energy ammonia synthesis be commercialised?

reflection: Haber, the savior of agriculture, also developed chlorine gas for WWI; his wife killed herself in despair. How should we judge the morality of dual-use chemistry?
